https://www.dw.com/en/sicily-mount-etna-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NPtd Catania lies in the foothills of Mount Etna, flights to the city are frequently disrupted by the active volcano Image: Salvatore Allegra/Anadolu/IMAGO Advertisement Flight restrictions at Italy 's Catania Aiport were extended on Monday, following disruptions to services over the weekend. A thick ash cloud emanating from the nearby Mount Etna volcano has prompted authorities to halt flights. What do we know about the disruption? The Sicilian aiport's operator, SAC, said that all flight operations at the hub had been suspended until at least midnight local time (2200 GMT/UTC) on Monday night. It said that where possible arrivals and departures were transferring to Sicily's other airports in Palermo and Comiso. Catania is Italy's fifth-busiest airport, and Sicily's largest hub. Catania airport said that where possible, flights were diverting to Sicily's other airports, Palermo or Comiso Image: Salvatore Allegra/Anadolu/IMAGO SAC advised passengers to check the status of their flights prior to setting off for the airport. The Mediterranean island is a popular holiday destination but travelers have faced frequent disruptions this summer because of eruptions and more commonly because of ash emanating from Etna. Ash from the northeast crater of the mountain is being carried southward by the wind. Italian Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV) said the ash did not appear to indicate an imminent explosive phase. What is Mount Etna? Mount Etna is a roughly 3,400 meter (roughly 11,100 feet) stratovolcano on Sicily's eastern coast. Its precise height is ever changing, particularly amid periods of high activity when it can shed a few meters. The city of Catania is located not far to the south. Despite the dangers, settling near volcanoes also has advantages like rich soil, hence Catania's success down the centuries Image: Salvatore Allegra/Anadolu/IMAGO Etna is one of the tallest active volcanoes in Europe and Italy's highest peak south of the Alps. It's in an almost constant state of low-level activity and erupts in a more pronounced manner fairly frequently. It has caused disruptions at Catania airport several times this year, and in recent years . A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the first volcanic activity took place at Etna about half a million years ago. Both Roman and Greek mythology asserted that the god of blacksmithing — either Vulcan or Hephaestus — had his forge beneath Mount Etna. https://www.newswise.com/articles/czech-.text: Czech President Pavel to visit University of Nebraska–Lincoln Newswise — Czech President Petr Pavel will visit the University of Nebraska–Lincoln on Sept. 24 for a campus conversation highlighting the longstanding cultural and educational ties between Nebraska and the Czech Republic. Pavel will meet with University of Nebraska–Lincoln Interim Chancellor Katherine S. Ankerson and Dr. Jeffrey P. Gold, president of the University of Nebraska system, before participating in a moderated discussion with the campus community at Kimball Recital Hall. The conversation will focus on Nebraska’s Czech heritage, educational and cultural exchange, and the transatlantic relationship between the two countries. “President Pavel’s visit is an opportunity to recognize the longstanding ties between Nebraska and the Czech Republic and the important role the University of Nebraska–Lincoln has played in that relationship,” Ankerson said. “For more than a century, our university has been a place where Czech language, culture and scholarship have connected generations. “We are honored to welcome President Pavel and to continue building our educational and cultural connections.” The event will begin at 11 a.m. Sept. 24 in Kimball Recital Hall, 1113 R St. Tickets are required and seating is limited. Learn more about how to access free tickets . The University of Nebraska established formal Czech language instruction in 1907, following years of efforts by Czech-American students, community members and state lawmakers. Nebraska was among the first universities in the United States to offer Czech language instruction. The roots of the program date to 1904, when Nebraska students established the Czech Komenský Club to promote the study and preservation of Czech language and culture. Czech immigration has played a significant role in Nebraska’s history. Beginning in the 19th century, immigrants from Bohemia and Moravia established communities statewide, contributing to Nebraska’s cultural, agricultural and civic life. The connections created by those communities continue through cultural organizations, academic programs and exchanges between Nebraska and the Czech Republic. Today, the university is one of the few across the nation to offer Czech language instruction and opportunities for students to study and engage with Czech culture. The university offers students more than 25 different study abroad opportunities. The university also maintains Czech Heritage Collections documenting the history and experiences of Czech Americans. Visiting students from the Czech Republic find additional support at Nebraska, including the Paul Robitschek Scholarship , available to international exchange students affiliated with an accredited postsecondary institution in the Czech Republic. The scholarship was created by Robitschek, a Czech immigrant who came to the United States and built a successful career in chemical and plastics manufacturing. Pavel was elected president of the Czech Republic in January 2023 and took office that March. Before becoming president, he served more than three decades in the Czech military, including as chief of the General Staff of the Czech Armed Forces. From 2015 to 2018, he served as chairman of the NATO Military Committee. The event will be livestreamed for those unable to attend in person. More information, including details on parking and clear bag policy, is available online . Pavel’s visit is part of a larger tour of Nebraska. He will also meet with Gov. Jim Pillen and tour Wilbur, Nebraska. https://www.politico.eu/article/publishe.text: BRUSSELS — Europe’s biggest media companies have asked regulators in Brussels and London to stop Meta from introducing new terms they say would let it copy publishers’ websites to build artificial intelligence, as a backlash that began in the U.S. spreads across Europe. In a letter Monday, the European Publishers Council, whose members include POLITICO’s owner Axel Springer, called on EU competition boss Teresa Ribera and tech chief Henna Virkkunen to press Meta to put the terms on hold before they take effect Oct. 30. The group wants Brussels to check them against EU copyright and competition law, and has requested an urgent meeting with the teams of both commissioners. Advertisement Advertisement “The Commission remains committed to ensure that Meta’s practices fully comply with all applicable obligations under EU law, including competition rules and the Digital Markets Act,” Commission spokesperson Ricardo Cardoso told POLITICO, referring to the EU’s rulebook for Big Tech. He said Brussels was aware of both Meta’s changes and publishers’ concerns. The U.K. competition watchdog has moved as well. British publishers have complained to the Competition and Markets Authority that Meta is so dominant they are compelled to accept its terms. The watchdog’s chief, Sarah Cardell, told British lawmakers on Tuesday that it had asked Meta to explain the changes and would meet the company on Wednesday. She named Meta as a possible candidate for Britain’s new rules for tech giants. Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), speaks in a panel discussion during the Annual CBI Conference, at Queen Elizabeth II Centre on November 25, 2024 in London. | Leon Neal/Getty Images The terms cover businesses that use Meta’s tools to run Facebook pages, Instagram accounts or ads, which includes almost every newsroom. The fight began in the U.S. last week, when Nieman Lab, a journalism research outlet at Harvard, reported on the terms after receiving a tip from a small business owner. As first written, they let Meta send automated programs to copy websites linked to those accounts and use the material to “train” its products, Nieman Lab concluded. There is no opt-out, and a business that continues to use Meta’s tools after Oct. 30 will be deemed to have consented. Advertisement Advertisement Publishers say the terms would hand Meta content for free that other AI companies pay to license. Rapid reaction On Friday, Meta communications chief Andy Stone responded on X that the Nieman Lab report was “false” and that there was “no change to how Meta uses web crawlers.” Stone said the update aimed to let Meta pull accurate product information from shopping sites for ads, not to scrape news sites. The company also said the crawling language already existed in other Meta terms and was just being gathered in one place. Late Friday, however, Meta revised the terms and deleted the word “train,” saying the terms cover only its advertising and business products. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify,” a spokesperson for Meta told POLITICO over the weekend, adding the change was “not about scraping news sites.” Publishers say that changes little, however. Advertisement Advertisement Meta has given them verbal assurances that they can keep using its tools without surrendering their content to AI, but the terms themselves don’t guarantee that, the European Publishers Council’s letter says. “Meta’s supposed Friday night correction is a farce,” said Jason Kint, who heads Digital Content Next, a U.S. publisher group whose members include Axel Springer. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.” Others have gone further. “This is unscrupulous theft,” Germany’s newspaper and magazine associations said in a joint statement on Tuesday. They want Brussels to block the terms while it reviews them, warning that once articles are copied into AI systems, they can’t be clawed back. Joseph Bambridge in London contributed reporting.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn0.text: Image source, Russian military Image caption, The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack By Paul Kirby Europe digital editor Published 8 hours ago Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike. Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast. The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes. Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war. Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast. The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic. Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables. Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed. Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg." The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details. "The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group. Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation. Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia. Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace. He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia. Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones. Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".
